figures.bridge_line: the Persian sage whose dated letters survive where his life does not - a voice from inside the persecution

dates.floruit: Demonstrations 1-10 dated 336/337; 11-22 dated 344; 23 dated August 345 - written inside the Persian empire, traditionally associated with the Adiabene region

names.name: Aphrahat (fl. 337-345; 'Mar Jacob, the Persian sage' in the 510 colophon; the name Aphrahat first attested tenth century)

figures.bridge_line: the brilliant court philosopher this world's chief singer spent his life answering - kin enough to argue with, far enough to refuse

dates.born: 154 (the Chronicle of Edessa records his birth date)
dates.floruit: courtier and philosopher at the court of Abgar VIII 'the Great' (r. 177-212); Julius Africanus met him there (195)

figures.bridge_line: the deacon-poet who taught the faith by singing it - and spent his last year nursing famine victims

dates.born: c. 306 (scholarly convention; Nisibis or its territory, per Sozomen)
dates.died: 373, at Edessa (Jerome: 'died in the reign of Valens'; the famine-relief tradition places his last public act shortly before)
dates.floruit: Nisibis until the 363 cession, then Edessa 363-373; deacon (Jerome De viris; Palladius; Griffith 1986)

figures.bridge_line: the bishop the besieged city remembered praying on its walls

dates.died: 338 vs 350 - the Martyrologium Hieronymianum implies 338 (the first siege), the Chronicon Paschale has him defending Nisibis in 350; a genuine primary-source conflict, held open and never resolved either way
dates.floruit: bishop of Nisibis from c. 309; signatory at Nicaea (325); the city's intercessor in the Persian sieges; traditionally Ephrem's own bishop and baptizer

names.name: Jacob of Nisibis (bishop from c. 309; at Nicaea 325; died 338 or 350 - a genuine primary-source conflict)

figures.bridge_line: the frontier bishop whose embassies opened the door the Persian church walked through in 410

dates.floruit: bishop of Maiperqat in Roman Mesopotamia; envoy between the Roman court and Yazdegerd I; his access helped secure royal permission for the synod of 410; remembered for gathering the relics of the persecution's martyrs

names.name: Marutha of Maiperqat (Martyropolis), Roman bishop and imperial envoy to Yazdegerd I (fl. c. 399-410s)

figures.bridge_line: the bishop whose claim to lead all Persia's bishops was fought in his own lifetime - proof the hierarchy was real, and unsettled

dates.floruit: bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon around the turn of the fourth century; his claim to primacy over other Persian bishops was fiercely contested by Miles of Susa and Aqib-Alaha of Karka d'Baith Slok at a synod c. 315

names.name: Papa bar Aggai, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon (fl. c. 280s-310s; primacy claim contested c. 315)

figures.bridge_line: the bishop just past this world's horizon, under whom its one woven Gospel gave way to the four

dates.floruit: bishop of Edessa 411-435: the generation after this world's window closes; traditionally credited with the Diatessaron-to-Peshitta shift and the suppression of the remaining Bardaisanite and Marcionite communities

names.name: Rabbula, bishop of Edessa 411-435 - JUST PAST this world's own boundary

figures.bridge_line: the bishop who told the King of Kings he would not worship the sun - and led his clergy to death first

dates.died: traditionally 341; Kosinski and Burgess argue c. 344 - the anchor date for the whole chronicle-derived succession, held open and never resolved either way
dates.floruit: bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in the opening of the Great Persecution

names.name: Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon (martyred under Shapur II; traditional date 341, disputed - c. 344 argued)

figures.bridge_line: the man who wove the four Gospels into the one story these churches read for two hundred years

dates.floruit: student of Justin at Rome; returned east c. 172; the harmony spread through the Syriac-speaking churches

names.name: Tatian the Assyrian (fl. c. 160-180; the Diatessaron composed c. 172)
